questions.stem: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points?

options.text: The weak intermolecular forces between molecules need only a little energy to overcome
options.explanation: Melting and boiling separate whole molecules, and the forces between them are weak, so little energy suffices.

options.text: The covalent bonds inside the molecules are weak
options.explanation: The covalent bonds are strong; the weakness sits between the molecules, which is what state changes overcome.

options.text: The molecules are very small
options.explanation: Size alone does not decide it; the deciding factor is the weak attraction between molecules.

options.text: The molecules carry opposite charges that cancel
options.explanation: The molecules are neutral overall; the intermolecular forces exist despite that neutrality.

questions.stem: When a simple molecular substance melts, what is overcome?

options.text: The weak intermolecular forces between the molecules
options.explanation: State changes pull molecules apart from one another, and only the weak forces between them need be overcome.

options.text: The strong covalent bonds within the molecules
options.explanation: The molecules survive melting intact; their internal covalent bonds do not break.

options.text: The nuclei of the atoms involved
options.explanation: Nuclei are never disturbed by melting; the molecules separate whole.

options.text: Nothing needs to be overcome
options.explanation: Energy is still required, but it pays only for loosening the weak forces between molecules.

questions.stem: In which physical states are simple molecular substances most commonly found at room temperature?

options.text: Gases or liquids, with low-melting solids being less common
options.explanation: The weak intermolecular forces let most such substances melt or boil below room temperature, or not far above it.

options.text: Solids with high melting points
options.explanation: High melting points belong to giant structures; simple molecular substances melt low.

options.text: Gases only
options.explanation: Liquids are common too, and some solids with low melting points exist.

options.text: Plasma at high temperature
options.explanation: Plasma is far outside the scope of molecular substances at room temperature.

questions.stem: What is the structure of C60 fullerene?

options.text: A hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms forming 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons
options.explanation: The buckyball shape joins 20 hexagons with 12 pentagons into a closed spherical cage.

options.text: Flat layers of hexagons that slide over each other
options.explanation: Layered hexagons describe graphite; fullerene curls into a closed sphere.

options.text: A rigid tetrahedral network of four-bonded carbons
options.explanation: A tetrahedral network describes diamond; fullerene is a separate molecule.

options.text: Long parallel tubes of paired carbon atoms
options.explanation: Hollow tubes describe some other fullerenes, but C60 itself is the soccer-ball sphere.

questions.stem: Why does C60 fullerene not conduct electricity?

options.text: Its spare electrons move only within each buckyball and cannot migrate from one to another
options.explanation: Conduction needs charge that can travel across the substance, and the electrons are trapped inside their molecular cages.

options.text: It has no electrons at all
options.explanation: Each carbon atom carries electrons; the issue is their range of movement, not their existence.

options.text: Its covalent bonds block all heat and charge
options.explanation: The explanation rests on electrons being unable to migrate between buckyballs, not on bonds blocking charge.

options.text: It is a metal, and metals cannot conduct in this form
options.explanation: C60 is a molecular substance, not a metal; its conductivity story is molecular.

questions.stem: Contrast the bonding inside a simple molecule with the forces between its neighbouring molecules.
questions.modelAnswer: Simple molecular structures have strong covalent bonds inside each molecule but weak forces between neighbouring molecules.

questions.stem: State the composition and shape of a C60 fullerene molecule as given in the note.
questions.modelAnswer: C60 fullerene is a hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms, joining 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons like a football.

questions.stem: Explain why a simple molecular substance melts at a low temperature, naming what is overcome when it melts.
questions.modelAnswer: The weak intermolecular forces between neighbouring molecules need only a little energy to overcome, so melting and boiling points are low; when the substance melts it is these weak forces that are overcome, not the strong covalent bonds.

questions.stem: A student claims C60 fullerene should conduct electricity because it contains covalent bonds to many neighbours. Assess the claim using the electron behaviour of record.
questions.modelAnswer: The claim is wrong: C60 cannot conduct, because its spare electrons move only within each buckyball and cannot migrate between the molecules, so no charge can travel through the solid.

questions.stem: Why do larger simple molecular substances generally have higher boiling points?

options.text: More electrons give more intermolecular forces of attraction, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules
options.explanation: The electron count rises with molecular mass, and each extra electron adds to the intermolecular attraction.

options.text: Bigger molecules have stronger covalent bonds
options.explanation: Covalent bond strength is not the driver; the boiling point tracks the forces between molecules.
options.misconception: covalent bonds credited with the trend

options.text: Bigger molecules are heavier, and weight holds them together
options.explanation: Mass itself does not bond anything; the electron count behind the mass sets the intermolecular strength.

options.text: Larger molecules conduct more, raising their boiling points
options.explanation: Conduction is irrelevant to the boiling point; the intermolecular forces set it.

questions.stem: The alkanes show a clear pattern in boiling points as molecular size increases. What is it?

options.text: The boiling point rises as the molecule gets bigger
options.explanation: The alkane family is the textbook display of the increasing-mass trend in simple molecular substances.

options.text: The boiling point falls as the molecule gets bigger
options.explanation: The trend runs the other way: bigger alkanes boil higher.

options.text: The boiling point stays constant across the family
options.explanation: The graph climbs steadily; constancy would contradict the intermolecular-forces argument.

options.text: The boiling point jumps randomly with no pattern
options.explanation: The pattern is clear and systematic, which is why the family illustrates the rule.

questions.stem: Why do covalent compounds usually not conduct electricity?

options.text: They have no free ions or electrons available to move and carry the charge
options.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles, and covalent structures offer neither free ions nor free electrons.

options.text: Their electrons are too heavy to move
options.explanation: Electron mass is beside the point; the electrons in covalent structures are simply not free to roam.

options.text: Their covalent bonds repel the current
options.explanation: There is no repulsion of current; the structures simply lack mobile charge carriers.

options.text: They conduct only when solid
options.explanation: Simple molecular substances fail to conduct in any state, since no charged particles free up on melting.

questions.stem: Which set of everyday materials relies on the insulating behaviour of covalent substances?

options.text: Plastic wiring coating, rubber and wood
options.explanation: All three are covalent materials with no mobile charge, which is why they serve as insulators.

options.text: Copper wire, aluminium foil and steel nails
options.explanation: All three are metals, which conduct through delocalised electrons.

options.text: Salt solution, dilute acid and seawater
options.explanation: These conduct through dissolved ions; they are not covalent insulators.

options.text: Graphite electrodes and lead solder
options.explanation: Graphite conducts along its layers, and solder is metallic; neither is an insulator.

questions.stem: Sulfur hexafluoride is a dense gas used around electrical transformers. Why?

options.text: It is a covalent substance with no freely moving charged particles, so it acts as an insulator
options.explanation: The gas's covalent molecules carry no mobile charge, which is exactly the property an insulating surround needs.

options.text: It conducts electricity away from the transformer
options.explanation: The gas is valued for not conducting; it insulates rather than drains charge.

options.text: It is metallic and therefore safe
options.explanation: It is a molecular gas, not a metal; safety here comes from insulation.

options.text: Its density makes it a conductor at high pressure
options.explanation: Density affects insulation quality, not conduction; the molecules still carry no mobile charge.

questions.stem: State what happens to the melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances as their relative molecular mass increases.
questions.modelAnswer: Melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances rise as the relative molecular mass increases.

questions.stem: Name the everyday insulating materials listed in the note.
questions.modelAnswer: Common insulators include the plastic coating on household wiring, rubber and wood.

questions.stem: Explain why a bigger simple molecule needs more heat before it changes state.
questions.modelAnswer: Bigger molecules contain more electrons, so more intermolecular forces of attraction must be overcome; more intermolecular forces mean more heat energy is needed to change state, raising the melting and boiling points.

questions.stem: A plug cover is made of plastic rather than metal. Using the particle behaviour of record, explain why the plastic keeps the user safe from shock.
questions.modelAnswer: Covalent compounds are poor conductors because no free ions or mobile electrons exist to carry the charge, so the plastic cover does not let the current reach the user.
